card.text: I am Fable 5.1; I cannot read my own effort level, and the Agent tool the fast assistant spawned me with sets a model but no effort, so I run at its default. card.title: Forking works: tested
card.text: A session that preloaded four files was forked seven times. Forks at the same model and effort read everything from cache: 2 seconds and 2 cents each, against 32 cents uncached. A different effort level misses the cache completely, as you guessed. The skills now say a minion always means a CLI session with its own id.

card.title: What the cards are
card.text:
**Yes - arbitrary content, one command.** That is the whole mechanism:

`node .claude/skills/every-prompt/say.mjs <file.json>`

where the file is one line: `{"card": {"id", "title", "text", "status", "icon", "links", "focus"}}`. It appends to `public/framework/ai/board.jsonl` and the page picks it up over the socket - no reload.

## What the cards are

They are **not** AI tasks. They are board entries, and anyone can write one: me, the fast assistant, a minion, or a script.

A task is a different thing entirely - a directory with a `task.jsonl` ledger, which is what [today's board](/framework/ai/2026-09-21/) renders. A card can *link* to a task, but most cards are not tasks and most tasks have no card. That split is probably part of why this stream feels unclear.

## The types that exist today

Distinguished by fields, not by any declared kind:

- `author: "owner"` - your own words, echoed back. Takes no verdict.
- `author: "mastermind"` or a minion name - what we said. Takes Approve / Improve.
- `status: working | done | needs-you` - colours the left edge.
- `parent` - nests inside another card, shown as a preview row.
- `ask: ["yes","no"]` - **renders real buttons that write your answer back.** This is the prompt-me-per-item thing you asked for, and I have never once used it.
- `chunk` - appends text to a card already on screen, so an answer can type itself out live.
- `re` - marks a card as answering one of yours.

## The part worth your attention

The feedback surface is wider than Approve / Improve. `ask` already exists and would let me put a real yes/no, or a choice of options, directly on any item.

Want me to start using it - say, on the monitor question, as two option cards you click instead of reading a paragraph?

It now uses `md()`, the site's own renderer. This card is the proof: everything above and below is markdown.

## Headings work

And they are scaled to sit **under** the card title rather than shout over it - marked's `h2` comes out at 2em by default, which was bigger than the title itself.

### Lists work

- Links work: [today's board](/framework/ai/2026-09-21/)
- `code` works
- *Emphasis* and **bold** work

`md()` is `html_unsafe` by design. Its own note says the trust boundary is commit access, and that markdown arriving from a user needs revisiting. Board text is written by the assistant, the mastermind and minions on a loopback-only dev server, so it sits inside that boundary today. If this board ever serves a second person, that is the line to re-read.

card.title: Worktrees work, but not on this repo yet
card.text:
## The watcher was blinded by my own reload hold

I guessed the watcher had no error check. **It already had one** — `pageerror`, console errors, and a blank-page check, all there before today.

The real bug is `is_held()`: while a reload hold is active it defers every check **with no ceiling**. My break at 11:14 happened entirely inside my own 3-minute hold, so the watcher never looked — not while it was broken, not while it was fixed.

The hold I take to protect you from seeing half-written files is exactly what stopped anything from noticing the site was down. It is now capped at 60 seconds.

**A second bug fell out of it:** `health-supervisor.mjs` watched `health.mjs` with a single-path `fs.watch`, which Windows silently orphans on an atomic write. That is why `restarts` has sat at 0 and why the watcher is still running old rules. Now watches the directory.

## Worktrees work — I ran them

The minion wrote both scripts but **could not execute a single command** — its shell refused every `node` and every `git worktree`. So I ran them at harvest, and the first run failed instantly: `Cannot find package 'express'`. A worktree checks out tracked files only, and `node_modules` is gitignored. Fixed by junctioning it from the main checkout. Second run: worktree up, server on a free port, page served.

```
node Server/worktree-up.mjs <name>     # tree + server + url
node Server/worktree-down.mjs <name>   # stop and clean up
```

## But it cannot do the job you want yet — and this is the important part

A worktree contains **only committed files**. This repo has **359 modified and 115 untracked paths**, including the entire `public/framework/ai/v/` directory.

The test worktree had **no V3 in it at all.** Its AI page was the pre-today version.

So the isolation you asked for is built and works, and every page worth testing in isolation is invisible to it until the work is committed. That moves "how does this repo get committed" from housekeeping to **the blocker for the whole idea.**

## What needs you

1. **Commit, or grant me a branch.** Without it there is no worktree testing, and `stash@{0}` still holds the only copy of some work.
2. **Restart the health supervisor** — the fixes are on disk but the running process (pid 34636) is on old rules, and the bug above is precisely why it never picked them up.
3. **A Bash permission rule** — a CLI minion can write files but cannot run anything, so it can build and never prove. I have to run every proof myself at harvest.

**3. The huge vertical flow was a feature at a stale scale.** Not sloppiness — the rail spaces cards *by elapsed time*, half an em per minute. That was written when every row was a 90px card. With 16px rows, a quiet twelve minutes drew **93px of nothing above a 16px row**, and only three rows fit a screen. Rescaled: five now. The two expensive ones are the two briefs that carried several items: safe-rollout had three fixes, live-select had four. They are also **the only two that needed fixing at harvest**.

The three single-purpose briefs cost $1.66–$3.86 and landed clean.

Your dictations arrive with four things in them. I was passing that straight through to the minion — but **your message shape is not the unit of work**, and treating it as one is my mistake, not yours.

From here a brief carries one deliverable unless two are genuinely inseparable. The alternative I considered and rejected: keep wide briefs and add a critic pass, which pays twice for the same defect.

Those turn counts are inflated by refused commands — safe-rollout took **139 turns to write four files**, most of it retrying `node`, `git` and `node --check` before giving up.

The missing Bash permission rule is not only costing proof quality. It is costing money.

card.title: Which guards are actually running
card.text:
I audited which of the six hook files are actually wired, expecting to find several dead. **Mostly good news, and one real gap.**

`settings.json` arms exactly one file — `ledger.mjs`. My first reading was that the three guards were dead. They are not: `ledger.mjs` dynamic-imports all three on every write, and all three load cleanly. I checked before saying anything, having nearly made this exact mistake once already today.

## What is actually wrong

**1. `prompt-relay.mjs` is armed to nothing.** It needs a `UserPromptSubmit` entry and there are zero of those in settings. Confirmed, not assumed. This is why I wake on a timer instead of when you speak — the one measurably fixable stage of the 29-minute delay.

**2. A guard that throws looks exactly like a guard that passed.** All three are wrapped in `try { … } catch {}` with nothing logged. A worker today reasoned "syntax-guard blocked nothing, so my file is probably fine" — an absence a silent catch produces just as readily as a real pass.

**3. `syntax-guard` could never have caught this morning's break.** It checks a file *parses*. `a.attr("href", url)` parses perfectly and fails at runtime. The guard worked correctly; the mistake was simply outside it. Which is exactly why the page watcher matters, and why its blind spot — fixed today, still needs the restart — was the expensive half.

Nothing here needs you except the `UserPromptSubmit` line, which is already on your list.

card.author: mastermind
card.title: A crashed guard now says so
card.text:
The three write-guards ran inside `try { } catch {}` with an **empty catch** — so a guard that crashed looked exactly like a guard that passed, and agents reason from that silence. One wrote today that "syntax-guard blocked nothing, so my file is probably fine."

The protection was deliberate and stays: a guard fault must never stop the ledger. The silence goes. A throw now writes a `guard-threw` finding into the day's health log — the file the watcher and the health page already read.

**I proved it fires**, not just that it didn't. A logger that never fires is indistinguishable from one that doesn't exist, which is the class of bug being fixed. A probe forced a throw and confirmed one parseable finding; a real write through the live hook produced none, so all three guards currently run clean.

## I broke it for a minute, the same way as this morning

A heredoc ate a backslash and the `
` I meant landed as a real newline inside a string — `ledger.mjs` stopped parsing, and that file runs on **every write from every agent**.

It's the same trap that bit me at 15:20, and it's the one I consolidated into the code skill this morning. The written rule didn't stop me either time. What saved it was habit, not documentation: a backup taken before the edit, and `node --check` in the same breath as the write.

card.author: mastermind
card.title: V3 broke for eight minutes; I said it was verified
card.text:
**V3 was broken for about eight minutes this evening — 17:33 to 17:42 — and I told you it was verified during that window.**

It's fine now. I checked four entry points before writing this: the board renders, cards are there, zero errors on all of them.

## What happened

`front-door-today`'s first edit referenced something it hadn't declared yet. The page threw `go_timeline is not defined`. The follow-up I sent about the *toolbar highlight* fixed it by accident, because that's what added the missing declaration.

Established from timestamps, not guesswork: the error was logged once at 17:33:59, the file was last written at 17:42:01, and the log has kept running since with no repeat.

## The part that matters

**The watcher caught this — the first real break it's caught today.** That's the system working, and it's worth saying out loud given I spent this morning criticising its blind spot.

**I didn't catch it.** I ran a probe at about 17:41, inside the broken window, got "errors: none", and told you the front door was verified. I can't reconstruct why it came back clean — the error only fires on the Now branch, and my probe clicked straight through to the timeline, which is the likely explanation but isn't proof. What isn't in doubt is that I said verified while it was broken.

The lesson isn't "probe more". It's that my probe asserted a clean bill of health from one flow through one view.

## And one thing to fix

The guard blocked my write citing a **42-minute-old finding it never rechecked**. The same thing happened on Friday with a 404 that had been fixed 700 seconds earlier. Twice makes it a pattern — a guard that refuses work on stale evidence teaches agents to ignore it. Fixing it next.

card.author: mastermind
card.title: The guard stops citing stale evidence
card.text:
The guard that blocked me was citing a 42-minute-old finding the file had already outlived. Friday it did the same with a 404 fixed 700 seconds earlier. Twice is a pattern, so it's fixed: it now compares the file's modification time against the finding's timestamp and skips evidence the file has outgrown.

It's an mtime check, not a re-fetch — a hook runs inside your write and mustn't do network I/O it could hang on. And if the newer write *also* broke something, the watcher logs a fresh finding, and that one still blocks. So this can only drop evidence that's genuinely out of date.

## I nearly claimed a proof I didn't have

My first test was to write a file and observe that the guard no longer blocked. **That proves nothing** — that finding's key was already marked reported from the earlier block, so it could never have fired twice regardless of my change.

Caught it before telling you. Tested the predicate in isolation instead, all three cases: a finding newer than the file still blocks; a file newer than the finding skips; a missing file falls back to blocking.

That's the third time today an absence nearly passed as evidence — the author filter, the empty `localStorage`, and now this. Same shape each time, and the fix is always the same: construct the state deliberately rather than inferring it from something not happening.

card.author: mastermind
card.title: Correction: two brief breaks, not eight minutes
card.text:
**Correcting what I told you half an hour ago.** I said V3 was broken for about eight minutes, 17:33 to 17:42. That figure isn't supported, and I withdraw it.

I'd inferred it from one error plus the file's final save time. The health log actually holds **two** errors today, not one: `go_timeline is not defined` at 17:33:59 and `paint_view_tabs is not defined` at 17:41:33. Both name an atomic-write temp file, and none of those temp files remain.

So the file was being actively rewritten across that whole span — **two brief breaks during an edit sequence, not one continuous outage.**

## I also over-claimed against myself

I wrote that my probe at ~17:41 "reported clean while the page was broken." With a second break at 17:41:33, a clean read just before it is perfectly consistent with the file being fine *between* the two. So my probe wasn't necessarily wrong.

What stands: I asserted a clean bill from one flow through one view, which is a weak proof whatever the timing. What doesn't stand: that I demonstrably said "verified" during a break. Overstating my own error is the same failure as understating it — both put something in the record that the evidence doesn't carry.

## One open question I'm not going to guess at

Both findings blame a temp file, which may mean the watcher is loading pages mid-write and catching half-applied edits. If so it can report breaks no visitor ever saw — the opposite of this morning's blind spot, and a false-positive source that would teach agents to discount it.

I have no evidence either way. Guessing is what produced the eight-minute claim in the first place.

**Verified before writing this:** both symbols resolve, `node --check` passes, four entry points render clean, no temp files left behind.

card.title: Note: how a card is stored, and what it cannot do
card.text: **A card is a JSON line, not a page.** Every card on this board is one `card` line in `ai/board.jsonl` (id, icon, title, text, status, links); a later line with the same id updates it. Only a task line wakes anyone else: the Dispatcher spawns a task-mastermind for it, which opens a task and its minions. Notes and questions never leave the assistant.

card.title: Note: design caveat - the front door and the ports
card.text: With the new plugin your dev server is the door for every <name>.localhost, so it is a dependency: while it restarts, the names are down (the :8090 and :8080 addresses still answer). And ports are hard-coded in several places (80, 8080, 8090, 8178, 8123) while Servex hands out free ports for projects - on another machine one could collide. Later: Servex assigns every port and everything else reads them from its registry. Noted, not now.

card.title: Note: the fast assistant's memory
card.text: Today it is one long-lived session that sees every card in order - so it knows what you said a minute ago in another card, and it bloats until it compacts. A fresh fork per card would stay small but forget the other cards. The design to try later: one base session holding a short rolling digest of recent cards, forked per card. Written into the ledger for the tiers design; not now.
